\chapter{Which Way}
\label{ch:ta-which-way}
\hlchaptermodality{66}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say up, down, inside, outside, right and left in Tamil, and put each one in front of a verb or a noun I already know.}

Complete TA-C66-whichway-recall and produce each of the six directions from its opposite, then sort all six by the ending they take.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mēlē]{\ta{மேலே} (mēlē) — up, above}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-up}



\begin{quote}
One word back from last chapter first: what did \emph{mūḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மேலே}}
\textbf{\ta{மேலே}} (\emph{mēlē}) — \textquotedblleft{}up, above\textquotedblright{}.

It sits in front of the verb, where every Tamil adverb sits: \textbf{\ta{மேலே} \ta{பார்}} (\emph{mēlē pār}) — \textquotedblleft{}look up\textquotedblright{}. You already have \ta{பார்} from the seeing lesson, so this is one new word buying you a whole instruction.

Underneath it is \textbf{\ta{மேல்}} (\emph{mēl}), the bare word for \textquotedblleft{}the top\textquotedblright{}, a native Dravidian positional word. Kannada says \textbf{\ka{ಮೇಲೆ}} (\emph{mēle}) for the same idea, and it is the same word, worn the same way.

\begin{culture}
Listen to the end of the word, and then say the two pointing words you already have. \textbf{\ta{இங்கே}} (\emph{iṅgē}, \textquotedblleft{}here\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\ta{அங்கே}} (\emph{aṅgē}, \textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{}) end the same way. That \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} is Tamil's way of turning a bare place-word into \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{at} that place, \textbf{to} that place\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{\ta{மேல்}} plus \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} is \textbf{\ta{மேலே}}, \textquotedblleft{}at the top, upward\textquotedblright{}.

So this is not a new machine. It is a machine you already own, running on a new word.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mēlē}
  \item \emph{mēlē pār} — \textquotedblleft{}look up\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{iṅgē}, \emph{aṅgē}, \emph{mēlē} — three words, one ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மேலே} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Up, above\textquotedblright{}.) What two pointing words end the same way, and what does that ending do? (\textbf{\ta{இங்கே}} and \textbf{\ta{அங்கே}} — the \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} makes a place-word mean \textquotedblleft{}at, or to, that place\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kīḻē]{\ta{கீழே} (kīḻē) — down, below}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-down}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{}, and the instruction you built with it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கீழே}}
\textbf{\ta{கீழே}} (\emph{kīḻē}) — \textquotedblleft{}down, below\textquotedblright{}. The other half of the pair, and built by the same two pieces: \textbf{\ta{கீழ்}} (\emph{kīḻ}, \textquotedblleft{}the bottom\textquotedblright{}) plus the \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} you met one lesson ago.

\textbf{\ta{கீழே} \ta{பார்}} (\emph{kīḻē pār}) — \textquotedblleft{}look down\textquotedblright{}. Same slot, same verb, opposite direction.

\begin{sounds}
The middle of this word is \textbf{\ta{ழ}} (\emph{ḻ}), the retroflex glide you first met inside \textbf{\ta{மகிழ்ச்சி}} and again in \textbf{\ta{தமிழ்}} itself. Curl the tongue back and let the air pass beside it; it is not an English \emph{l} and it is not an English \emph{r}.

The vowel in front of it is \textbf{long}: \emph{kīḻ}, not \emph{kiḻ}. Tamil separates words by vowel length, so the length is doing work here, not decoration.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kīḻē} — feel the \ta{ழ}
  \item \emph{mēlē pār}, then \emph{kīḻē pār}
  \item both bare words, \emph{mēl} and \emph{kīḻ}, then both with the ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கீழே} mean, and what two pieces build it? (\textquotedblleft{}Down, below\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\ta{கீழ்}} plus \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}}.) Which rare Tamil letter sits in the middle of it? (\textbf{\ta{ழ}}, the same one in \emph{tamiḻ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mēlē]{\ta{மேலே} — the same sign twice}

\label{lesson:TA-W22-read-mele}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons ago you learned to say \emph{mēlē}, and \emph{kīḻē} came between. Now look at it on the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: two letters, one sign, used twice}
Like \textbf{\ta{குடி}} before it, \textbf{\ta{மேலே}} brings no new shape. It brings something better: the same vowel sign riding two different letters, one after the other.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{மே}} & \emph{mē} — \textbf{\ta{ம}} with the \textbf{\ta{ே}} sign & \textbf{\ta{ம}} from the letter-\emph{ma} lesson; the \textbf{\ta{ே}} sign from the vowel-sign lesson, and again inside \emph{pēsu} \\
\textbf{\ta{லே}} & \emph{lē} — \textbf{\ta{ல}} with the \textbf{\ta{ே}} sign & \textbf{\ta{ல}} from the letter-\emph{la} lesson; the \textbf{same} \textbf{\ta{ே}} again \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{மே} · \ta{லே} $\to$ \ta{மேலே}}
\end{quote}

Read it once as two beats. Both beats are long, and both are long for the same reason: the \textbf{\ta{ே}} hook in front of each letter.

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: the hook goes in front, the sound comes after}
The \textbf{\ta{ே}} sits to the \textbf{left} of the letter it belongs to, and is said \textbf{after} it. \textbf{\ta{மே}} is written hook-then-\textbf{\ta{ம}} and read \emph{mē}. That is not a quirk of this word — it is how this sign has always worked, and \textbf{\ta{மேலே}} shows it twice in a row so you can watch the eye do it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{மே}} — then \textbf{\ta{லே}} — then \textbf{\ta{மேலே}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} the \textbf{\ta{ே}} in each of the two beats
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{மேலே}}, then say the instruction you built from it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{மேலே}}. How many times does the \textbf{\ta{ே}} appear, and on which side of its letter does it sit? (\textbf{Twice}; on the \textbf{left}, though it is said after.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uḷḷē]{\ta{உள்ளே} (uḷḷē) — inside}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-inside}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{மேலே}} off the page, and then say its opposite.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{உள்ளே}}
\textbf{\ta{உள்ளே}} (\emph{uḷḷē}) — \textquotedblleft{}inside, in\textquotedblright{}.

The same shape a third time: \textbf{\ta{உள்}} (\emph{uḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}the inside\textquotedblright{}) plus the \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} that turns a place-word into a place you can go to.

And now it earns its keep. \textbf{\ta{உள்ளே} \ta{வா}} (\emph{uḷḷē vā}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{come in}.\textquotedblright{} That is what a Tamil household says at the door, and you have had \textbf{\ta{வா}} since the coming-and-going lesson. One new word, and you can answer a doorway.

\begin{culture}
Written out, \textbf{\ta{உள்}} ends in the retroflex \textbf{\ta{ள்}}, and the ending brings a second one: \textbf{\ta{உள்} + \ta{ஏ} $\to$ \ta{உள்ளே}}, with \textbf{\ta{ள்ளே}} doubled in the middle. Hold it a beat longer than a single \ta{ள}, the way you already hold the \emph{kk} in \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}.

You have met that doubling before without being told it was the same thing: \textbf{\ta{வெள்ளை}} (\emph{veḷḷai}, \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{}) carries it too.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uḷḷē} — hold the doubled \ta{ள}
  \item \emph{uḷḷē vā} — \textquotedblleft{}come in\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{mēlē}, \emph{kīḻē}, \emph{uḷḷē} — three place-words, one ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{உள்ளே} mean, and what do you say at a door with it? (\textquotedblleft{}Inside\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\ta{உள்ளே} \ta{வா}}, \textquotedblleft{}come in\textquotedblright{}.) What happens to the \ta{ள} when the ending arrives? (It \textbf{doubles}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veḷiyē]{\ta{வெளியே} (veḷiyē) — outside}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-outside}



\begin{quote}
What do you say at a door to bring someone in?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வெளியே}}
\textbf{\ta{வெளியே}} (\emph{veḷiyē}) — \textquotedblleft{}outside, out\textquotedblright{}. The answer to \ta{உள்ளே}, and the fourth word built the same way: \textbf{\ta{வெளி}} (\emph{veḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}the open, the outside\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}}.

\textbf{\ta{வெளியே} \ta{போ}} (\emph{veḷiyē pō}) — \textquotedblleft{}go out\textquotedblright{}. Put it beside \textbf{\ta{உள்ளே} \ta{வா}} and you have a matched pair of instructions, each one an old verb with a new word in front of it.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ta{உள்}} ends in a consonant, so \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} doubled it. \textbf{\ta{வெளி}} ends in a vowel, and two vowels cannot sit against each other, so Tamil slides a \textbf{\ta{ய்}} (\emph{y}) between them: \textbf{\ta{வெளி} + \ta{ஏ} $\to$ \ta{வெளியே}}.

Tamil grammar has a name for that sliding letter: \textbf{\ta{உடம்படுமெய்}} (\emph{uḍambaḍumey}), the \textquotedblleft{}body-joining consonant\textquotedblright{}. Its whole job is to stand between two vowels that would otherwise meet, and it is either \textbf{\ta{ய்}} or \textbf{\ta{வ்}}. Once you know it is there, you stop hearing \textbf{\ta{வெளியே}} as a word with a strange extra letter and start hearing it as \textbf{\ta{வெளி}} with an ending on it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{veḷiyē}
  \item \emph{uḷḷē vā}, then \emph{veḷiyē pō}
  \item the bare pair — \emph{uḷ} and \emph{veḷi} — then both with the ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two instructions does this pair give you at a door? (\textbf{\ta{உள்ளே} \ta{வா}}, \textquotedblleft{}come in\textquotedblright{}, and \textbf{\ta{வெளியே} \ta{போ}}, \textquotedblleft{}go out\textquotedblright{}.) Why is there a \textbf{\ta{ய}} inside \ta{வெளியே} and not inside \ta{உள்ளே}? (\textbf{\ta{வெளி}} ends in a \textbf{vowel}, so a \textbf{\ta{ய}} slides in to keep two vowels apart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[valadu]{\ta{வலது} (valadu) — the right side}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-right}



\begin{quote}
Say the pair you can use at a door.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வலது}}
\textbf{\ta{வலது}} (\emph{valadu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the right side, the right-hand one\textquotedblright{}.

It does not take the \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} ending, because it is not that kind of word. It goes straight in front of a noun: \textbf{\ta{வலது} \ta{கை}} (\emph{valadu kai}) — \textquotedblleft{}the right hand\textquotedblright{}. You have had \textbf{\ta{கை}} since the head-and-hand lesson, so again the new word is the only new thing.

\begin{culture}
Listen to how it ends, and say the two pointing words again — this time the pair that names things rather than places. \textbf{\ta{இது}} (\emph{idu}, \textquotedblleft{}this one\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\ta{அது}} (\emph{adu}, \textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{}) end in the same \textbf{-\ta{து}}. That ending means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the one that is}\textquotedblright{} — so \textbf{\ta{வலது}} is, quite literally, \textquotedblleft{}the right one\textquotedblright{}.

Two endings from the same stretch of the book, and now you can hear the machine from both sides: \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} makes a \textbf{place} you can move to, \textbf{-\ta{து}} makes a \textbf{thing} you can point at.

\begin{quote}
Tamil's word for the right side sits close to \textbf{\ta{வலி}} (\emph{vali}), \textquotedblleft{}strength\textquotedblright{} — the strong hand naming the side, a link many languages make (English gets \emph{dexterity} from the Latin for \textquotedblleft{}right\textquotedblright{}). Take that as the usual account rather than a settled derivation.
\end{quote}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{valadu}
  \item \emph{valadu kai} — \textquotedblleft{}the right hand\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{idu}, \emph{adu}, \emph{valadu} — three words, one ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{வலது} mean, and what does it not take that \ta{மேலே} does? (\textquotedblleft{}The right side\textquotedblright{}; it takes \textbf{no -\ta{ஏ}}.) Which two pointing words share its ending? (\textbf{\ta{இது}} and \textbf{\ta{அது}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[iḍadu]{\ta{இடது} (iḍadu) — the left side}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-left}



\begin{quote}
Which hand is the \textbf{\ta{வலது} \ta{கை}}? Hold it up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இடது}}
\textbf{\ta{இடது}} (\emph{iḍadu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the left side, the left-hand one\textquotedblright{}. The last of the six, and it behaves exactly like \ta{வலது}: no \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}}, straight in front of the noun. \textbf{\ta{இடது} \ta{கை}} (\emph{iḍadu kai}) — \textquotedblleft{}the left hand\textquotedblright{}.

Both hands, in two words you can now hold up and check against each other.

\begin{culture}
Written out, \textbf{\ta{இடது}} carries \textbf{\ta{ட}} between two vowels — and you learned in the reading lesson for \textbf{\ta{குடி}} that a \textbf{\ta{ட}} in that position softens. So the book writes this word \emph{iḍadu}, not \emph{iṭadu}, for the same reason it writes \emph{kuḍi} and \emph{eppaḍi}. One letter, read by where it stands.

\begin{quote}
Tamil's word for the left side looks a great deal like \textbf{\ta{இடம்}} (\emph{iḍam}), \textquotedblleft{}place, room\textquotedblright{} — and dictionaries do connect them. Treat that as the usual account rather than a settled fact; it is the kind of link that is easy to see and hard to prove.
\end{quote}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{iḍadu}
  \item \emph{valadu kai}, then \emph{iḍadu kai} — and raise each hand as you say it
  \item all four of the \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} words, then both of the \textbf{-\ta{து}} words
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{இடது} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The left side\textquotedblright{}.) Why is its \textbf{\ta{ட}} read as a soft \emph{ḍ}? (Because it sits \textbf{between two vowels}, the same rule as in \emph{kuḍi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The six directions, retrieved}

\label{lesson:TA-C66-whichway-recall}



\begin{quote}
Reach back one chapter first: what did \emph{tiṟa} mean, and what did \emph{mūḍu} mean? Nothing new arrives in this lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — retrieve, do not recite}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the word for \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{}, and the instruction that sends the eyes there
  \item the word for \textquotedblleft{}down\textquotedblright{}, and the same instruction pointed the other way
  \item what you call at a door to bring someone in
  \item all four of the \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}} words, in the order you met them
  \item all four again, fastest you can hold them
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the pairs, out of order}
Each prompt names one half. Say the other.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kīḻē} $\to$ {[}PAUSE 2s{]} (\emph{mēlē})
  \item \emph{veḷiyē} $\to$ {[}PAUSE 2s{]} (\emph{uḷḷē})
  \item \emph{iḍadu} $\to$ {[}PAUSE 2s{]} (\emph{valadu})
  \item \emph{uḷḷē vā} $\to$ {[}PAUSE 2s{]} (\emph{veḷiyē pō})
  \item \emph{mēlē pār} $\to$ {[}PAUSE 2s{]} (\emph{kīḻē pār})
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{மேலே}}, then say the verb that goes after it
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — sort the six}
Two endings, and every word in this chapter takes one of them.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Sort:} which four take \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}}, and which two take \textbf{-\ta{து}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} why the four go in front of a \textbf{verb} and the two go in front of a \textbf{noun}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ta{வலது} \ta{கை}}, then \textbf{\ta{இடது} \ta{கை}}, raising each hand
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of the six never take \textbf{-\ta{ஏ}}, and what do they take instead? (\textbf{\ta{வலது}} and \textbf{\ta{இடது}} — the \textbf{-\ta{து}} of \textbf{\ta{இது}} and \textbf{\ta{அது}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
